name: Cognitive Load
description: The amount of mental effort required to understand what an interface is saying and how to use it. Interfaces feel harder when they force users to hold, compare, or interpret more than working memory comfortably supports.
design_relevance_note: A core lens for simplifying navigation, forms, error states, dashboards, and multi-step flows by removing unnecessary interpretation, memory work, and competing stimuli.
prevalence_note: Appears both as a dedicated Laws of UX concept and throughout NN/g's usability canon; 'reduce cognitive load' is one of the most pervasive explanatory phrases in day-to-day UX critique and design review.

findings.description: When a learning or problem-solving task requires more cognitive processing capacity than working memory can supply (e.g. conventional means-ends-analysis problem solving), that excess load leaves insufficient capacity for schema acquisition — the foundational basis for cognitive load theory, and for the now-common design guidance to minimize unnecessary cognitive burden in interfaces and instructional material.
findings.source_title: Cognitive Load During Problem Solving: Effects on Learning

applications.title: Adobe presenting a complicated pricing page immediately after a trial click
applications.description: Adobe presents new users with multiple subscription tiers, confusing bundle-versus-standalone price comparisons, and unclear value propositions immediately upon clicking to try the product -- before the user has had any chance to experience the actual feature they came to explore.
applications.ethical_note: Not a deceptive pattern on its own, but front-loading complex pricing decisions before any product value is experienced imposes a real cost on the user's decision-making capacity at the least-informed point in their journey -- worth distinguishing from a pure accidental-usability-flaw case, since the sequencing (pricing before product) is a deliberate flow design choice.

applications.title: Audible requiring mental math to compare credit-based and direct pricing
applications.description: Audible's credit-bundle pricing requires a customer to calculate whether using a credit (priced at $14.95) or paying directly for a specific book (priced at $12.99) is the better value -- forcing arithmetic during a purchase decision rather than presenting a clear, directly comparable price.
applications.ethical_note: Requiring mental math to compare a proprietary credit currency against a real cash price is a mild but real form of price obfuscation, even if unintentional -- distinct from a pure accessibility/complexity failure, since a currency-conversion step specifically obscures the actual cost being compared.

applications.title: Etsy suggesting relevant alternatives based on a user's search input
applications.description: Etsy surfaces multiple relevant alternative products based on what a user has already searched for, reducing the mental effort of independently generating and evaluating other options to consider.
applications.ethical_note: A genuine convenience feature that reduces search effort -- no evidence of steering users toward higher-margin or sponsored alternatives specifically, just input-relevant suggestions as described in the source.

applications.title: Google Analytics communicating setup progress with an explicit indicator
applications.description: Google Analytics shows users an explicit progress indicator during a multi-step setup process, clearly communicating how far along they are rather than leaving them to track their own progress mentally.
applications.ethical_note: A pure orientation aid with no persuasive angle -- telling a user where they are in a process they already chose to start.

applications.title: Hopper's over-saturated, overly granular flight-date price color-coding
applications.description: Hopper's date-selection calendar used highly saturated colors across many narrow price bands (as little as $50 apart) to indicate flight pricing, creating visual complexity that made it harder, not easier, for users to quickly tell cheap dates from expensive ones.
applications.ethical_note: A visual-design complexity issue with no persuasion angle -- too much color-coded information makes a decision harder to parse, it doesn't push the decision in any particular direction.

applications.title: Slack organizing its checkout form into clearly labeled sections
applications.description: Slack's checkout form is divided into distinct sections (organization info and payment method) rather than presenting every field as one undifferentiated list, reducing the mental effort needed to understand what information is being requested and why.
applications.ethical_note: A structural clarity improvement with no persuasion angle -- grouping related fields helps a user understand a form faster, it doesn't shape their decision about what to buy.
